title: A Undertow for the Glasshouse
premise: After her mother's funeral, Yara Pemberton returns to the family glasshouse to catalog a lifetime of unspoken things, including the sentence she has rehearsed for five years and never delivered. When a radio plays an unreleased song her mother wrote for someone Yara has never heard of, she is pulled into the hidden life behind the silence, tracing a found family of musicians who loved her mother in ways Yara never witnessed. As the glasshouse is scheduled for demolition, Yara must finally translate the unsayable sentence — that she saw what happened the night her mother's music ended, and stayed quiet out of loyalty. She speaks it at last, trading the family's comfortable silence for a harder, truer kind of belonging.
about_author: Paloma Reyes is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging other people's letters before writing her own. She lives near the coast, where she collects unfinished songs and the stories people almost tell.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Almost
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Days after the funeral, Yara begins cataloging the glasshouse — seed ledgers, unlabeled tapes, her mother's locked writing desk. The emotional beat is numb grief sharpened by the realization that she knew her mother least of anyone. She finds a lyric sheet dated the year before Yara was born, unsigned.

chapters.title: A Song That Was Never Sung
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. In a diner, a radio plays a song Yara knows was never recorded — her mother's melody, someone else's voice. Shaken, she tracks the station and learns the singer, Marisol Vega, performs weekly at a coastal bar. The beat is vertigo: the past asserting it exists.

chapters.title: Marisol
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara confronts Marisol after a set; Marisol recognizes her instantly as 'the daughter,' revealing a twenty-year friendship Yara never knew of. Marisol is warm but guarded, warning that some things were kept from Yara for reasons. The beat is longing mixed with suspicion.

chapters.title: What the Glasshouse Kept
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Yara in the present, fragments of her mother Odile's journal interleaved. Yara learns the glasshouse was a rehearsal space for a band called Undertow, and that Odile wrote every song but let others take credit. The beat is dawning betrayal on both sides of the timeline.

chapters.title: The Fourth Chair
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Marisol introduces Yara to Theo and Bram, the surviving bandmates, now estranged from each other. Each tells a different version of why Undertow dissolved the night of a fire no one will describe. The beat is competing loyalties; truth begins to look like a matter of allegiance.

chapters.title: Five Years of Practice
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, with flashbacks. We learn what Yara has almost said for five years: she was there as a teenager the night the studio burned, and she saw who struck the match. Her silence bought her mother's forgiveness — or so she believed. The beat is guilt surfacing like a body in water.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo confesses his own version: Odile was leaving the band, taking the songs, and he burned the master tapes rather than lose them. He believes Odile forgave him; Yara realizes her mother carried two silences, one for each of them. The beat is devastating symmetry.

chapters.title: Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The glasshouse demolition is moved up; inside, Yara finds Odile's final letter, addressed to her, unfinished mid-sentence — the same sentence Yara has been practicing. Marisol urges her to finish it aloud before the walls come down. The beat is urgency compressing grief into decision.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Climax. Yara's POV. At a farewell gathering in the glasshouse, with Marisol, Theo, and Bram present, Yara speaks the sentence she saw: not Theo's hand with the match, but her mother's — Odile burned it herself, and Yara's five-year silence protected a fiction everyone needed. The beat is rupture and release.

chapters.title: What Grows in Broken Glass
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, epilogue. The glasshouse falls, but the four of them record the never-recorded song together in its ruins' echo, finishing Odile's unfinished letter as liner notes. Yara stops practicing sentences and starts saying them. The beat is quiet resolution: truth costs everything and returns a family.
